Neonates of the Bolivian big-eared mouse emerge into the world at a remarkably modest size, with newborn pups weighing approximately 1.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.5 grams]. This low birth mass, typical of many altricial rodent species, reflects a trade-off where the energetic demands of gestation in the high-altitude environments of the Bolivian Altiplano are balanced against the need to produce a sizable litter. Such a small initial body mass likely imposes significant thermoregulatory challenges on the altricial neonate, underscoring the critical role of lactation in early survival. The thermoneutral zone for these small mammals, as determined in laboratory respirometry trials, is found at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]; under these stable thermal conditions, the pups are sustained entirely by the mother's milk. This period of complete dependence on maternal provisioning is brief but vital, lasting until the offspring begin to transition to solid food.

Under laboratory conditions maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], weaning occurs approximately 20 days after birth [tx = approximately 20 days after birth], a seemingly early age that is nonetheless sufficient for the pups to have developed the dentition and digestive capacity necessary to process solid items. This weaning time is a critical juncture in the life history, as it marks the cessation of lactation and the beginning of the juvenile's independent foraging. The timing of this dietary shift is tightly linked to the thermal environment, with the stable body temperature observed in the laboratory thought to reflect the optimal conditions that allow for such a rapid developmental schedule. Following weaning, the young animals enter a period of rapid somatic growth, during which mass gain accelerates as they exploit seasonally available seeds and vegetation. This post-weaning phase sets the stage for the subsequent maturation of the reproductive system.

The transition from juvenile to reproductively viable adult is marked by the attainment of sexual maturity at 26 days after birth [tp = 26 days after birth] when maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This rapid maturation, among the fastest recorded for similar-sized cricetid rodents, allows for a remarkably young age at first reproduction and contributes to the species' high intrinsic rate of population increase. The onset of gametogenesis and the first oestrus cycle are tightly coupled to this developmental timeline. By the time females reach this post-pubertal stage, their body mass has increased considerably from the neonatal value, with the typical adult body mass plateauing at around 55 grams [Wwi = around 55 grams]. Field-caught specimens often range between 21 and 51 grams depending on seasonal resource availability, illustrating considerable intraspecific variation in this ultimate wet weight.

Reproductive output in this species is channeled through litters of moderate size, which contributes to the rapid turnover that characterizes high-altitude rodent populations. Females typically produce litters containing between 3 and 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 3 and 5 pups per litter], and they are capable of producing approximately 4 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 4 litters per year] under favorable conditions. This annual reproductive frequency reflects a short gestation period, which lasts only 18 days [tg = only 18 days] when the mother's core temperature is held at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The combination of moderate litter size with a rapid gestational schedule allows females to produce a substantial number of offspring over the course of a single breeding season, an adaptation to the brief and unpredictable growing season in the high-elevation puna grasslands.

The basal metabolic rate of Auliscomys boliviensis, measured in resting animals under thermoneutral conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], is 110.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 110.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value is relatively high for a rodent of its adult body mass of 55 grams [Wwi = 55 grams], a pattern consistent with the demands of living in a cold, oxygen-thin environment where maintaining thermoregulation is energetically expensive. Despite this high metabolic throughput, the species exhibits a surprisingly extended lifespan for a small mammal of its size; maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated at approximately 5.3 years [am = approximately 5.3 years] when measured at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This lifespan is notably greater than would be predicted by simple allometric scaling equations, suggesting the presence of physiological mechanisms that mitigate oxidative damage associated with its elevated metabolism.

Life history theory predicts a trade-off between high metabolic rate and extended longevity, yet the Bolivian big-eared mouse appears to confound this expectation by combining a comparatively elevated basal oxygen consumption with an unexpectedly long lifespan. The stable core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] recorded under laboratory conditions is typical for small endotherms, but the ability to maintain somatic homeostasis across a five-year span while sustaining high metabolic throughput suggests unique cellular resilience. This species thus offers a compelling model for studying the physiological basis of slow senescence in small mammals adapted to extreme environments, where the selective pressures of cold temperatures and low oxygen availability may have shaped a novel coupling of metabolic and longevity traits.
